To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relative electrophoretic mobilities of the species in a protein‐DNA system depend on the number and type of protein molecules bound to DNA, the number and type (configuration) of DNA sequences occupied, and the conformation of the macromolecular complexes.

the intensities of electrophoretically separated species are determined by the equilibrium distributions of complexes, and that the intensities are proportional to the concentrations of species that are not retarded.

(1) the relative electrophoretic mobilities of protein‐DNA species are determined by the relative mobilities of their components; (2) the electrophoretic mobility of a protein‐DNA complex is not necessarily a simple function of the mobilities of its components; (3) the relative electophoretic mobility of protein‐DNA complex species depends on the configuration of the protein‐DNA complex, and on the macromolecular conformations of both the protein and the DNA;
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theoretical framework for the quantitative interpretation of the electrophoretic behavior of protein‐DNA mixures.
understanding the mechanisms that control the assembly of macromolecular complexes in solution, and with developing methods that can be applied to the study of such systems.
the analysis of the molecular interactions that determine the equilibrium distribution of species in protein–DNA mixtures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

native gel electrophoretic analysis is a powerful and useful technique that has the potential to provide important insights into the molecular mechanisms that govern the interactions of proteins with DNA.

the method of native gel electrophoretic analysis is a powerful technique that allows the determination of equilibrium constants, and the stoichiometries and conformations of protein‐DNA interactions in solution.
native gels are a very useful technique for studying protein‐DNA interactions, and that their use should become more widespread.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

electrophoretic mobility is determined by a complex function of the stoichiometric composition of the species present in the sample, and that the band intensity of any particular band is determined by the equilibrium constant for the association of its component protein(s) and DNA(s).
the electrophoretic behavior of interacting systems is determined by the equilibrium distributions of protein‐DNA species in the sample.

the electrophoretic analysis is an effective tool for the analysis of protein‐DNA interactions, but that it requires a careful interpretation of the data, which is often complicated by the presence of multiple interacting species and the non‐ideal behavior of the gel matrix.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the analysis of electroporetograms (band intensities) is a powerful tool for studying protein‐DNA interactions, provided that the underlying theory is understood and properly applied.

the analysis of band intensities can provide quantitative information on the thermodynamic properties of protein‐DNA interactions, provided the electrophoretic conditions and the protein concentrations are chosen appropriately.

, under favorable conditions, electrophoretic analysis can be used to determine the equilibrium constants for the formation of all possible species in a mixture, including species that are not present in the sample.
